title: Why RAG? Grounding LLMs in Your Data
summary: An LLM only knows what was in its training data, so it invents plausible-sounding answers when asked about your private documents or anything newer than its cutoff. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) fixes this by first retrieving relevant passages from your own data and then asking the model to answer using those passages — grounding the response, cutting hallucination, and letting you cite sources.

subtopics.title: Why models hallucinate
subtopics.explanation: An LLM is a next-token predictor trained to produce fluent text, not to know facts, so when it lacks the answer it still generates something confident and plausible. It has no built-in way to say 'I don't have that document' — it fills the gap with its best guess. This gap between fluency and factuality is the exact problem RAG is built to close.
subtopics.example:
# The model was never shown your internal wiki
question = "What is our Q3 refund policy for enterprise accounts?"
answer = llm([{"role": "user", "content": question}])
# -> 'Enterprise refunds are processed within 30 days...'
# fluent, confident, and completely made up: it has no such policy in weights

subtopics.title: Private and fresh data are missing from the weights
subtopics.explanation: Two things are permanently absent from a model's parameters: your private data (internal docs, tickets, code) which it never saw, and anything after its training cutoff (last week's release, today's prices). No amount of clever prompting recovers information the model was never trained on. Getting that data in front of the model at answer time is precisely what retrieval provides.
subtopics.example:
cutoff = "2024-10"
query_date = "2025-06"
# Anything about events after the cutoff is unknown to the weights
if query_date > cutoff:
    # the model cannot know this from training alone
    context = retrieve("latest pricing changes")  # must be supplied at runtime
    answer = llm_with_context(query, context)

subtopics.title: Retrieve then generate
subtopics.explanation: RAG is two steps: a retriever finds the most relevant passages for the question, then those passages are pasted into the prompt so the generator answers from them instead of from memory. The model's job shifts from 'recall a fact' to 'read this text and answer' — a task it is far better at. This retrieve-then-generate split is the entire core idea of RAG.
subtopics.example:
def rag_answer(question):
    passages = retrieve(question, k=3)      # 1) find relevant chunks
    context = "\n\n".join(passages)
    prompt = (
        f"Answer using ONLY the context below.\n\n"
        f"Context:\n{context}\n\nQuestion: {question}"
    )
    return llm([{"role": "user", "content": prompt}])  # 2) generate from it

subtopics.title: Faithfulness and citations
subtopics.explanation: Because the answer is derived from retrieved passages, you can instruct the model to stay faithful to them and to attach the source of each claim. This makes answers checkable — a user can click through to the exact document — and lets you detect when the model strays beyond its evidence. Grounding plus citation is what turns an LLM from a confident guesser into a source you can audit.
subtopics.example:
passages = [
    {"id": "doc-42", "text": "Enterprise refunds: 14 days, prorated."},
]
prompt = (
    "Answer using the context and cite the source id in [brackets].\n"
    f"[{passages[0]['id']}] {passages[0]['text']}\n"
    "Q: What is the enterprise refund window?"
)
# -> 'Enterprise refunds are within 14 days, prorated [doc-42].'

subtopics.title: When RAG beats fine-tuning
subtopics.explanation: Fine-tuning bakes behavior and style into the weights but is a poor fit for facts that change or must be cited, because retraining is slow and the source is lost inside the parameters. RAG keeps knowledge in an external store you can update instantly, filter by permissions, and trace back to a document. When the need is fresh, private, or auditable knowledge, RAG is usually the right tool — and it's the foundation the rest of this track builds on.
subtopics.example:
# Knowledge that changes or must be cited -> RAG
add_document(store, "pricing-2025-06.md")   # instantly available, no retrain

# Fixed behavior/format/tone -> fine-tuning
# e.g. 'always answer as a terse SQL expert' -> train that style in
# You can also combine both: fine-tune the style, retrieve the facts

foundations.overview: A large language model stores a compressed snapshot of its training data in its weights, which means it cannot know your private documents or anything that happened after its cutoff — and when asked anyway, it produces fluent, confident hallucinations rather than admitting ignorance. Retrieval-Augmented Generation solves this by splitting the work in two: a retriever pulls the passages most relevant to the question from an external store of your data, and the generator answers using those passages placed directly in the prompt. This shifts the model from unreliable recall to reliable reading comprehension, dramatically improving faithfulness, and because every answer traces back to specific retrieved passages you can cite sources and audit claims. RAG is often preferable to fine-tuning when knowledge is fresh, private, or must be attributable, since the external store updates instantly and preserves provenance. Understanding this retrieve-then-generate loop makes every later topic — embeddings, chunking, vector stores, and hybrid search — fall into place.
foundations.formalDefinition: Retrieval-Augmented Generation is a technique that, given a query, first retrieves relevant documents from an external knowledge source and then conditions an LLM's generation on both the query and the retrieved documents, so the output is grounded in supplied evidence rather than solely in model parameters.
foundations.whyItMatters: The highest-value questions people ask systems are about their own data and current events — exactly what a static model cannot know. RAG is what lets an LLM answer accurately about private, changing knowledge while showing its work, which is the difference between a chatbot that guesses and one an enterprise can trust.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of the LLM as a brilliant open-book exam taker with amnesia about your specific course: on its own it bluffs, but hand it the right pages first and it answers correctly and cites the page. RAG is the librarian that fetches those exact pages before the exam begins.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Customer-support bots answering from a help center, internal 'chat with your docs' assistants over wikis and PDFs, coding assistants grounded in a repo, legal and medical tools that must cite sources, and search experiences that summarize results with links.
commonUseCases: Question answering over private documents and wikis
Support assistants grounded in a help center
Answering about data newer than the model's cutoff
Cited, auditable answers for regulated domains

commonMisconceptions.myth: A bigger or newer model removes the need for RAG.
commonMisconceptions.reality: No model, however large, can contain your private data or events after its cutoff. Scale improves reasoning, not knowledge of documents it never saw — you still have to retrieve them.

commonMisconceptions.myth: RAG guarantees the answer is correct.
commonMisconceptions.reality: RAG grounds the answer in retrieved passages, but if retrieval returns the wrong passages or the model strays from them, it can still be wrong. Quality depends on retrieval quality and faithful prompting.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Fine-tuning is just a better version of RAG.
commonMisconceptions.reality: They solve different problems. Fine-tuning teaches behavior/style and can't be updated or cited easily; RAG supplies fresh, private, attributable facts. Often you combine them.

checkpoints.prompt: Why does an LLM hallucinate a confident answer about your internal refund policy?
options: It is intentionally lying to save compute
It is a fluent text predictor with no built-in way to signal 'I never saw that document', so it fills the gap
The API stripped the correct answer
checkpoints.explanation: An LLM predicts plausible next tokens; it has no internal flag for missing knowledge, so instead of abstaining it generates a fluent guess. RAG supplies the missing document so the model can read instead of guess.

checkpoints.prompt: Which question is RAG most necessary for?
options: Summarize the meaning of this paragraph I pasted
What did our sales deck published yesterday say about pricing?
checkpoints.explanation: The pricing deck is private and newer than any training cutoff, so the model cannot know it from weights — you must retrieve the passage at answer time. The others need no external, private, or fresh data.

checkpoints.prompt: When is RAG generally a better fit than fine-tuning?
options: When you want to change the model's tone/style permanently
When knowledge is fresh, private, or must be cited and updated often
When you need the model to run faster
When you have no data at all
checkpoints.explanation: RAG keeps knowledge in an external store you can update instantly, filter by permissions, and trace to a source — ideal for fresh, private, auditable facts. Fine-tuning is better for fixed behavior or style.

keyTakeaways: LLMs store a static snapshot of training data, so they can't know your private documents or anything after their cutoff — and they hallucinate instead of admitting it.
RAG = retrieve then generate: fetch the most relevant passages first, then have the model answer from them rather than from memory.
Grounding in retrieved text improves faithfulness and lets you cite the exact source of each claim, making answers auditable.
Prefer RAG over fine-tuning when knowledge is fresh, private, or must be attributable; prefer fine-tuning for fixed behavior or style (and combine when useful).
RAG quality is only as good as its retrieval — the rest of this track (embeddings, chunking, stores, hybrid search) is about retrieving the right passages.
